title: The World of AI: AI Courses catalogue for research and learning
answer: This is The World of AI's AI Courses page, a catalogue of AI courses with level, audience, cost and verification notes. Its most useful claim is that the field's course options split between university graduate theory and industry code-first practice, so learners choose a style rather than a more rigorous source. It says 13 courses are tracked, 11 free, 3 with companion code, but later refers to ten courses, and it gives no enrollment or completion data.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this page, titled AI Courses, as part of its AI Research and Learning section. It is a catalogue of AI courses, curated by level and audience, with one verified source for each entry. The page states that it tracks 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, and that source links are re-verified daily. Its last verified date is 2026-09-27. It also describes the wider site search across laws, lawsuits, glossary, tools, companies, research library, MCP server registry, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators and weekly digests, and it carries a promotional footer for books, consulting services and a novel.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page says its course list is curated by level and audience, with one verified source each, and that the skills taught map to an AI Skills Graph. DeepLearning.AI on Coursera offers a beginner course for managers, executives and anyone working alongside technical teams, free to audit. A second DeepLearning.AI Coursera course is intermediate, free to audit with a paid certificate. Dataquest offers a beginner course for developers who want hands-on practice with LLM APIs. fast.ai offers a beginner to intermediate course for programmers and top-down learners, free, with companion code. DeepLearning.AI and Stanford on Coursera offer a beginner course, free to audit with a paid certificate. It says all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, though three pair that with a paid certificate option or public code repositories. It says four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry, DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. It argues university courses are structured around exam-driven theory while industry courses are code-first or hands-on, so the choice is about how someone wants to learn rather than which source is more rigorous. Only three courses list a public code repository, fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero and MIT's 6.S191. The data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates or which course is most widely taken. The headline count of 13 courses and 11 free conflicts with the later reference to ten courses tracked.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states 13 AI courses, 11 free, 3 with public companion code, and says source links are re-verified daily. It gives a last verified date of 2026-09-27 and course entry verification dates of 2026-09-26. It says all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, which conflicts with the headline count of 13. It names four university graduate courses with public materials: Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191. It names three courses with public code repositories: fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero and MIT's 6.S191. It says membership is editorial, based on significance not sponsorship, and that nothing is paid placement. It says the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates or which course is most widely taken. It also says skills map to an AI Skills Graph.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in Education can use this source as a dated catalogue of courses that the field's learners and workers might take, with level, audience, cost model, free access and code availability noted. Its most useful angle is the stated split between university graduate theory and industry code-first practice, which frames course choice as a learning-style decision rather than a quality ranking. It also points to an AI Skills Graph, suggesting the courses are meant to map to skills. Because it gives no enrollment, completion or outcome data, it is best used to see what is offered and how it is described, not to judge which course works best.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Education

sections.body: The page is a catalogue, not a study, and the harvested text gives only five course entries while claiming 13 courses. Its counts are inconsistent, with 13 courses and 11 free in the headline and ten courses tracked in the summary. It does not report enrollment, completion, learner outcomes or which course is most widely taken. It does not list duration or full cost details for every entry, despite saying courses include duration and cost. It is published by The World of AI and carries a promotional footer for books, consulting services, audits and a novel, so it has a commercial context even though it says membership is editorial and not paid placement. It is dated 2026-09-27 and may change because links are re-verified daily.
